   Proof of Theorem 1. We perform the elimination process for the generalized equation Ω = Ωv0
corresponding to G. If the process goes infinitely we obtain one of the following:
Groups with regular free length functions in Λ                                                      31


    • free splitting of G with at least on non-trivial free factor (4.4.1) and, maybe, some surface
      group factor (4.4.2),
    • a decomposition of G as the fundamental group of a graph of groups with QH-vertex groups
      corresponding to quadratic sections (4.4.4 (a)),
    • decomposition of G as the fundamental group of a graph of groups with abelian vertex groups
      corresponding to periodic structures ( see Proposition 3 in 4.4.4 (c)) and HNN-extensions with
      stable letters infinitely longer than the generators of the abelian associated subgroups (4.4.4
      (c)).
Then we continue the elimination process with the generalized equation Ωv0 where the active part
corresponds to weakly rigid subgroups. In the case of an HNN-extension the complexity τ (Ωv1 ) is
smaller than τ (Ωv0 ). In the other cases the Delzant–Potyagailo complexity of weakly rigid subgroups
is smaller by Proposition 2. Therefore this procedure stops. At the end we obtain some generalized
equation Ωvf in with all non-active sections. Continuing the elimination process till the end, we
obtain a complete system of linear equations with integer coefficients Σcomplete on the lengths of
items hi ’s that is automatically satisfied, therefore the associated maximal abelian subgroups are
length-isomorphic.
    Notice that if Gi+1 = GΩvi+1 is obtained as the fundamental group of a graph of groups with
two vertices, where Gi is one vertex group and the other vertex is a QH-vertex, then one can also
obtain Gi+1 from Gi by taking a free product of Gi and a free group and then the HNN-extension
with cyclic associated subgroups. If Gi+1 is an amalgamated product of Gi and a free abelian group
then it can be obtained from Gi as a series of extensions of centralizers.
    This completes the proof of Theorem 1.

Remark 5. If we begin with the group G   e mentioned in Remark 2 with free but not necessary regular
length function in Λ then in the Elimination process we work with the generalized equation Ω and
add a finite number of elements from G.  b Thus we got an embedding of G  e in a group that can be
represented as a union of a finite series of groups

                                     G1 < G2 < · · · < Gn = G,

where
    1. G1 is a free group,
    2. Gi+1 is obtained from Gi by finitely many HNN-extensions in which associated subgroups are
       maximal abelian and length isomorphic as subgroups of Λ.
Remark 6. As a result of the Elimination process, the equation Ωvf in (we will denote it Ωf in ) is
defined on the multi-interval I, that is, a union of closed sections which have a natural hierarchy: a
section σ1 is smaller than a section σ2 if the largest base on σ2 is infinitely larger than the largest
base on σ1 .
    The lengths of bases satisfy the system of linear equations Σcomplete .


5     Proof of Theorems 3 and 4
Suppose G, as above, is a Λ-free group with a regular action. Let Ω be a generalized equation
for G corresponding to the union of closed sections I, G = hM | Ω(M)i. Consider the Cayley
graph X = Cay(G, M) of G with respect to the generators M. Assign to edges of Cay(G, M) their
lengths in Λ and consider edges as closed intervals in Λ of the corresponding length. For each relation
Groups with regular free length functions in Λ                                                                  32


between bases of Ω, λi1 · · · λik = λj1 · · · λjm (without cancelation) there is a loop in X labeled by
this relation. Then the path on the boundary of this loop labeled by λi1 · · · λik has the same length
in Λ as the path labeled by λj1 · · · λjm . If x is a point on the path λi1 · · · λik at the distance d ∈ Λ
from the beginning of the path, and x′ is a point on the path λj1 · · · λjm at the distance d from
the beginning, then we say that x and x′ are in the same leaf. In other words, after we substitute
generators in M by their infinite word representations, we “fold” loops into segments. We consider
the equivalence relation between points of X generated by all such pairs x ∼ x′ . Equivalence classes
of this relation are called leaves. We also glue an arc isometric to a unit interval between each x
and x′ . Let F be the foliation (the set of leaves). One can define a foliated complex Σ = Σ(X, F )
associated to X as a pair (X, F ). We define a metric space T (X) as follows. The paths in Σ can
travel vertically (along the leaves) and horizontally (along the intervals in Λ). The length of a path γ
in Σ(X, F ) (denoted kγk) is the sum of the lengths of horizontal intervals in γ. The pseudo-distance
d between two points of Σ is defined as the length of a minimal path between them. A metric space
T is obtained from Σ by identifying points at pseudo-distance 0. We extend naturally the left action
of G on X to the action on T .
Lemma 19.        (1) T is a Λ-tree.
 (2) The left action of G on T is free.
Proof. We will prove the second statement first. Suppose x is a vertex of X, g ∈ G. Then gx is also
a vertex of X. If d(gx, x) = 0 in Σ, then x and gx are in the same leaf. Hence, there is a vertical
path x ∼ x1 ∼ · · · ∼ xk = gx that uses relations from Ω(M)

   R1 : p11 q11 = p12 µ1 q12 ,     R2 : p21 µ1 q21 = p22 µ2 q22 ,      ...,   Rk : pk1 µk−1 qk1 = pk2 qk2 ,

where all pij , qij are products of some bases (G is generated by bases from M); x is a vertex between
p11 and q11 , xi is a vertex on µi , xk is a vertex between pk2 and qk2 . Then µi = µi1 µi2 , where

ℓ(p11 ) = ℓ(p12 µ11 ), ℓ(p21 µ11 ) = ℓ(p22 µ21 ), . . . , ℓ(pi1 µ(i−1)1 ) = ℓ(pi2 µi1 ), ℓ(pk1 µ(k−1)1 ) = ℓ(pk2 ).

   Since relations are coming from the generalized equation Ω, p11 and p12 µ11 are the same infinite
words, as well as pi1 µ(i−1)1 and pi2 µi1 are the same infinite words for i = 2, . . . , k−1, and pk1 µ(k−1)1
                                                          −1
and pk2 are the same infinite words. Therefore µ11 = p12      p11 = p−1                       −1
                                                                     21 p22 µ21 , µ21 = p31 p32 µ31 , . . . ,
             −1             −1        −1          −1
µ(k−1)1 = pk1 pk2 and p12 p11 = p21 p22 . . . pk1 pk2 .
   Then p−1               −1                                    −1          −1
            k2 pk1 · · · p12 p11 = 1 in G. But the element pk2 pk1 · · · p12 p11 ∈ G takes gx ∈ X to

x ∈ X, hence pk2 pk1 · · · p12 p11 gx = x. Therefore gx = x and g = 1.
   If x is not a vertex of X, then x is a point on some edge of X labeled by µ0 and joining some x0
and x0 µ0 , while gx, by translation in the Cayley graph, is a point on the edge of X labeled by µ0
and joining gx0 and gx0 µ0 . There is a vertical path x ∼ x1 ∼ · · · ∼ xk = gx that uses relations of

R1 : p11 µ0 q11 = p12 µ1 q12 ,     R2 : p21 µ1 q21 = p22 µ2 q22 ,      ...,   Rk : pk1 µk−1 qk1 = pk2 µ0 qk2 .

Let y be a vertex of X belonging to one of the loops R1 , . . . , Rk and nearest to the leaf joining x
and gx. Suppose y belongs to the loop R2 and it is a vertex between p21 and µ1 . Then there is a
leaf joining y and gy that uses the relations R2 , . . . , Rk , R1 , and we can show that g = 1 as above.
    Now we prove that T is a Λ-tree. Suppose, we have a loop γ in Σ beginning at x, which is a
vertex of X (x ∈ V X). We are going to show that the image of this loop becomes degenerate in T (if
we remove all subpaths of the form pp−1 from the image of γ we get a point). Notice that the image
of any closed horizontal path in Σ is degenerate in T , so in the loop we can replace a horizontal
subpath joining any two vertices y, z ∈ V X by any other horizontal path joining y and z. Represent
γ = γ1 γ2 , where γ1 is a sequence of vertical and horizontal paths between x and another vertex y
Groups with regular free length functions in Λ                                                      33




                                                      or




                                    Figure 8: Replacing γ1 by γ3


of X, and γ2 is a horizontal path between y and x such that if there is a horizontal subpath p at
the end of γ1 then p does not contain another vertex z ∈ V X. We can use induction on the number
of vertical components in γ1 , the case of zero vertical components being trivial. We can replace the
path γ1 by a path γ3 of equal or shorter length with the same image in T such that each vertical
subpath of γ3 is passing through some vertex of X (see Figure 8).

    Let z1 ∈ V X be the first vertex of γ2 . Suppose the last vertical part of γ3 begins with z5 , ends
with z4 and is passing through z2 ∈ V X. Then the image in T of the circle at z2 consisting of
the vertical path from z2 to z4 (see Figure 9) and the corresponding horizontal path from z4 to z2
(denote it γ4 ) is degenerate. The image of the circle at z2 consisting of the vertical path from z2 to
z5 and the horizontal path z2 , z3 , z5 is also degenerate. Denote by γ5 the horizontal path between z3
Groups with regular free length functions in Λ                                                      34


and z2 . We now replace γ2 by γ5 γ4−1 γ2 and γ1 by the part of γ1 from x to z3 . The image of this path
in T is degenerate by induction because it has less vertical subpaths. Therefore, T is a Λ-tree.
    Similarly, we can construct a Λ-tree where G acts freely beginning not with the original gen-
eralized equation Ω but with a generalized equation obtained from Ω by the application of the
Elimination process. In this case we may have closed sections with some items hi with γ(hi ) = 1.
Then to construct the Cayley graph of G in the new generators we cover items hi with γ(hi ) = 1
by bases without doubles. (These bases were previously removed at some stages of the Elimination
process as matching pairs).
    Proof of Theorem 3. We begin by considering the union of the smallest closed sections, see
Remark 6. Denote the union of these sections by σ. The group H of the generalized equation
corresponding to their union is a free product of free groups, free abelian groups and closed surface
groups. Notice that for those sections for which γ(hi ) = 1 for some maximal height items, these
items hi are also products of some bases because initially every item is a product of bases. We can
assume the following:

  1. For all closed sections of σ such that γ(hi ) = 2 for all items of the maximal height, the
     number of bases of maximal height cannot be decreased using entire transformation or similar
     transformation applied from the right of the section (right entire transformation);
  2. For all closed sections of σ where we apply linear elimination, the number of bases of maximal
     height cannot be decreased using the transformations as above as well as transformation (E2)
     (transfer) preceded by creation of necessary boundary connections as in (E5) (denote it (E25 )),
     (E3) and first two types of linear elimination (D6) (denote it (D61,2 ));

    Indeed, if we can decrease the number of bases of maximal height using the transformations
described above then we just do this and continue. Since these transformations do not change the
total number of bases we can also assume that they do not decrease the number of bases of second
maximal height etc. We now re-define the lengths of bases belonging to σ in Rk . We are going to
show that all components of the length of every base can be made zeros except for the components
which appear to be maximal in the lengths of bases from σ.
    Let Ωσ be the generalized equation corresponding to the sections from σ. Let H be the group of
the equation H = hMσ | Ωσ (M )i.
    Denote by Λ1 the minimal convex subgroup of Λ containing lengths of all bases in σ, and by
Λ′ a maximal convex subgroup of Λ1 not containing lengths of maximal height bases in σ (it exists
by Zorn’s lemma). Then the quotient Λ1 /Λ′ is a subgroup of R. Denote by ℓ̂ the length function
in R on this quotient induced from ℓ. We consider elements of Λ′ as infinitesimals. Denote by Tb
the R-tree constructed from T by identifying points at zero distance (see [7], Theorem 2.4.7). Then
H acts on Tb. Denote by kγkR the induced length of the path γ in Tb, and by dR (x̄, ȳ) the induced
distance.
    However, the action of H on Tb is not free. The action is minimal, that is, there is no non-empty
proper invariant subtree. Notice that the canonical projection f : T → Tb preserves alignment, and
the pre-image of the convex set is convex. The pre-image of a point in Tb is an infinitesimal subtree
of T .
Lemma 20. The action of H on Tb is superstable: for every non-degenerate arc J ⊂ Tb with non-
trivial fixator, and for every non degenerate subarc S ⊂ J, one has Stab(S) = Stab(J).
   The proof is the same as the proof of Fact 5.1 in [18].
Lemma 21. Let σ1 be a closed section on the lowest level corresponding to a closed surface group
and the lengths of the bases satisfy some system of linear equations Σ. Then one can define the
lengths of bases in σ1 in Rk .
Groups with regular free length functions in Λ                                                     35


Proof. Denote by Mσ+ the set of bases (on all the steps of the process of entire transformation
applied to the lowest level) with non-zero oldest component and by Mσ0 the rest of the bases
(infinitesimals). Denote by ℓ̂ the projection of the length function ℓ to Λ1 /Λ′ as before. Then
λ ∈ Mσ+ if and only if ℓ̂(λ) > 0. We apply the entire transformation to σ1 . If we obtain an
overlapping pair or an infinitesimal section, where the process goes infinitely, we declare it non-
active and move to the right. This either decreases, or does not change the number of bases in the
active part. Therefore, we can assume that the process goes infinitely and the number of bases in
Mσ+ never decreases. Therefore bases from Mσ0 are only used as transfer bases.
    We will show that the stabilizer of a pre-image of a point, an infinitesimal subtree T0 of T is
generated by some elements in Mσ0 . An element h from H belongs to such a stabilizer if ℓ̂(h) = 0.
If some product of bases not only from Mσ0 has infinitesimal length (denote this product by g), then
the identity and g belong to leaves at the infinitesimal distance δ in Σ. Therefore using elementary
operations we can obtain a base of length δ. Denote by Λ′′ the minimal convex subgroup of Λ
containing all elements of the same height as bases from Mσ0 .
    This implies the following lemma which we need to finish the proof of lemma 21.
Lemma 22. Let σ 1 be the projection of the quadratic section σ1 to Λ1 /(Λ′′ ∩Λ1 ). Suppose the process
of entire transformation for σ1 goes infinitely and the number of bases in Mσ+ never decreases. Then
the process of entire transformation for σ 1 goes infinitely too and the number of bases in Mσ+ never
decreases.
    If ℓ(g) ∈ Λ′ then g is a product of bases in Mσ0 and ℓ(g) ∈ Λ′′ .
    This lemma implies that there is no element in H infinitely larger than all bases in Mσ0 , but
infinitely smaller than all bases in Mσ+ .
    Therefore, we can make all components of the lengths of bases in M zeros except for those
which are maximal components of some bases in M. Since M is a finite set, the number of such
components is finite, and the length is defined in Rk for some k not larger than the number of pairs
of bases.
    Let σ be a closed section corresponding to infinite linear elimination process for a free group as
in Lemma 7 (c). We cover (for technical reasons) items hi with γ(hi ) = 1 by bases without doubles.
(These bases were removed at some stages of the Elimination process as matching pairs).
Lemma 23. Let σ be a closed section corresponding to infinite linear elimination process for a free
group as in Lemma 7 (c). Let σ be the projection of section σ to Λ1 /Λ′′ . Suppose the process of
linear elimination on σ goes infinitely and some generalized equation Ω′ (with the minimal possible
number of bases) appears in this process infinitely many times. Then the process of linear elimination
on σ goes infinitely. Moreover, suppose for any base µ with ℓ̂(µ) = 0 obtained by elementary
transformations, ℓ(µ) ∈ Λ′′ . If H = hMσ | Ωσ (Mσ )i, and g ∈ H, ℓ̂(g) = 0 then ℓ(g) ∈ Λ′′ .
Proof. The first statement holds because the steps that we make in the process depend only on the
situation of bases of maximal height. If some product g of bases not only from Mσ0 has infinitesimal
length, then the identity and g belong to leaves at the infinitesimal distance δ in Σ. Therefore using
elementary operations we can obtain a base µ of length comparable to δ. Therefore δ ∈ Λ′′ .
Lemma 24. Let σ be a closed section corresponding to infinite linear elimination process for a free
group. Suppose the process of linear elimination on σ goes infinitely and some generalized equation Ω
(with the minimal possible number of bases) appears in this process infinitely many times. Suppose all
items have length in R. Then applying elementary transformations we cannot decrease the difference
k between the number of items and the total number of basic and boundary equations. This difference
is the rank of the free group that is the coordinate group of Ω.
Groups with regular free length functions in Λ                                                           36


Proof. Every equation Ω′ that is obtained from Ω by elementary operations has the free group of
rank k as the coordinate group. If we cut bases of Ω′ along boundary connections and start removing
eliminable bases, we have to remove them all. Every time when we remove eliminable base we express
one item in terms of the others. There must be k items left at the end.
    Lemma 24 implies that if σ is a closed section corresponding to infinite linear elimination process
for a free group, then a base µ with ℓ̂(µ) = 0 can only be obtained by elementary transformations
from bases in Mσ0 . Therefore, by Lemma 23, if H = hMσ | Ωσ (Mσ )i, and g ∈ H, ℓ̂(g) = 0 then
ℓ(g) ∈ Λ′′ .
    Finally, if a finitely generated abelian group H acts freely on a Λ-tree, then it is isometrically
embedded into Λ (see, for example, [3]).
Lemma 25. ([7],LLemma      L 1.1.6) If H is a finitely generated ordered abelian group, it has a decom-
position H = Λ1 . . . Λk for some k ≥ 0, where the ordering is the lexicographic ordering and
Λ1 , . . . Λk are subgroups of R.
   Therefore, H has a free basis h1 , . . . hk such that ht(h1 ) > . . . ht(hk ). We can now make all the
components in the length of the basis elements zeros except those corresponding to ht(h1 ), . . . , ht(hk ).
This defines a free length function in Rn on H. The new lengths of elements in H satisfy the same
system of linear equations as their lengths in Λ.
   Using induction on the number of levels obtained in the Elimination process, we similarly prove
the statement of Theorem 3.
   The points of an Rn -tree, where G acts freely are the leaves in the foliation corresponding to the
new length of bases in Rn . The new lengths of bases are exactly their Lyndon lengths. 
   Proof of Theorem 4. Notice that in the case when G       e is a finitely presented group with a free
length function in Λ (not necessary regular) it can be embedded in the group with a free regular
length function in Λ by Remark 2. That group can be embedded in R(Λ′ , X). When we make a
                          e we have to add only a finite number of elements from R(Λ′ , X). We run
generalized equation for G,
the elimination process for this generalized equation as we did in the proof of Theorem 1 and obtain
a group G as in Remark 5, where G   e is embedded, and then redefine the length of elements of G in
Rn as above. Therefore G acts freely and regularly on a Rn -tree. The theorem is proved.
   Moreover, using Lemmas 22 and 23, and induction one shows that the length function in Rn and
in Λ defined on G is regular. Therefore we proved Theorem 4.
Remark 7. If G  e is a finitely presented group which has a free (not necessary regular) length function
in Λ, then it acts freely on a Λ-tree, and one can construct, as in [4], a foliated band complex with
measured foliation with horizontal measure in Λ.
